shortDescription: In Antioch, Asia Minor and Rome, Christians met on Sunday, the Lord's day, to share bread and wine with thanks to God. Letters and messengers passing between their churches held them together.

timeline.when: Near the end of the 1st century
timeline.headline: Corinth removes some of its elders, and Rome's church writes to Corinth
timeline.witness: The letter of Rome's church, the only side of the quarrel that survives

lines.text: The church at Corinth asks Rome's church for its counsel. Rome's letter says sudden troubles at Rome have delayed its answer.

Corinth has removed some of its elders, the senior men who led the church together. Rome's letter says they served blamelessly, and blames envy and one or two persons who stirred the church against them.
Rome's letter argues that God sent Christ, and Christ sent the apostles. The apostles appointed bishops and deacons, the bishops' assistants, for those who would believe.

The apostles, Rome's letter says, foresaw strife over the bishop's office and ordered that approved men succeed them. Men appointed with the whole church's consent, who served blamelessly, cannot justly be removed.
Rome sends the letter by three messengers, Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus, to be sent back quickly with news of peace.
Irenaeus places the letter in the time of Clement, the third after the apostles to hold the bishop's office at Rome, and calls it a most powerful letter.
lines.note: Irenaeus wrote later, while Eleutherius was bishop of Rome.

timeline.headline: A short manual teaches the Two Ways, baptism and the thanksgiving
timeline.witness: The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, a short manual whose writer, date and place are unknown

lines.text: The manual opens on the Two Ways, one of life and one of death. The way of life is first to love God, who made you, and second your neighbor as yourself.
The manual tells its readers to share all things with a brother, and not to call them their own.

In the manual, newcomers are taught the Two Ways first. Then they fast for a day or two, and are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, in living water, or in other water if there is none.

The manual's prayers of thanksgiving, the eucharist, come first over the cup, then over the broken bread. As the bread was scattered over the hills and gathered into one, they pray, so may the church be gathered into God's kingdom. Only the baptized may eat or drink of it.
Every Lord's day, the manual says, its readers gather, confess their sins, break bread and give thanks. No one at odds with a neighbor joins them until the two are reconciled.
The manual's readers are to appoint their own bishops and deacons, and to test the traveling apostles who come to them. An apostle who stays three days, or asks for money, is a false prophet.

timeline.headline: A Roman governor questions Christians and writes to the emperor
timeline.witness: Pliny, the governor, a hostile outsider, in his letter to the emperor Trajan

lines.text: Pliny writes that Christians of every age and rank, and of both sexes, have spread through the cities, villages and countryside of his province.
lines.reference: Pliny, Letters 10.96.1 and 9, cic/texts/mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt lines 2768, 2799-2801; English, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 19509-19512

lines.text: Pliny does not know whether to punish the name Christian itself, or crimes that go with it. Those who confess it and hold firm, he has led away to punishment.
Some, named to Pliny by an informer, say they stopped being Christians, some as long as twenty years before, and curse Christ before him.

Those who have left tell Pliny they used to meet before dawn on a fixed day, sing a hymn to Christ as to a god, and bind themselves by oath against theft, robbery and adultery. Later they met again for an ordinary, harmless meal, and stopped after his order banning clubs.
To find the truth, Pliny has two slave women, called ministrae, servers, tortured. He says he found only a depraved superstition.
Jerome's Chronicle says that Pliny, while governing a province, had put very many Christians to death, and, alarmed at their numbers, asked Trajan what to do.
lines.note: Jerome wrote nearly three centuries later.

timeline.headline: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, writes to the churches on his way to Rome as a prisoner

lines.text: Ignatius writes that he has come bound from Syria for the common name and hope, and hopes to fight with beasts at Rome.
Eusebius says Ignatius travels through Asia under the strictest military guard, encouraging the churches of each city where he stops.
Ignatius writes from Smyrna, and later from Troas. He urges each church to act as one: its bishop presiding in the place of God, its elders in the place of the apostles' council, with its deacons.
lines.reference: Ignatius, To the Magnesians 15 and 6, To Polycarp 8, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 6219-6223, 5851-5856, 8854-8855

lines.text: A proper thanksgiving, Ignatius writes, is one the bishop leads, or one he entrusts to another. Where the bishop is, there let the people be.
Ignatius greets households: the families of his brothers with their wives and children, the house of Tavias, and the wife of Epitropus with all her house and children.
lines.reference: Ignatius, To the Smyrnaeans 13, To Polycarp 8, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 8503-8508, 8868-8869

lines.text: Ignatius hears that the church at Antioch in Syria is at peace. He asks Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, to choose a messenger to go to Syria, and to have the churches nearby send messengers or letters.

timeline.headline: Polycarp and the elders of Smyrna write to Philippi

lines.text: Polycarp's letter to the church at Philippi opens in his name and that of the elders with him.
lines.reference: Polycarp, To the Philippians, opening, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 3232-3235

lines.text: Polycarp writes that elders are to be compassionate and merciful, bring back those who wander, visit all the sick, and not neglect the widow, the orphan or the poor.
Polycarp grieves for Valens, once an elder at Philippi, who so little understands the place given him. He warns against love of money, and asks them to call Valens and his wife back.
As the Philippians asked, Polycarp sends them the letters of Ignatius his church holds, and offers to have their own letter carried to Syria. Crescens carries Polycarp's letter.

timeline.headline: Hermas writes down his visions at Rome
timeline.witness: Hermas, in his own book, the Shepherd

lines.text: In a vision, Hermas writes, the Church appears to him as an old woman. She tells him to make two copies of her words: one for Clement to send to foreign countries, and one for Grapte to teach the widows and orphans. Hermas is to read them in his own city, Rome, with the elders who preside over the church.
lines.note: A vision, in Hermas's own voice.

lines.text: In Hermas's book, bishops gladly take God's servants into their houses, and care for the widows and those in need.

timeline.headline: Justin tells the emperor how Christians at Rome baptize and keep Sunday
timeline.witness: Justin, a Christian teacher at Rome, in the defense of the Christians he addressed to the emperor

lines.text: Justin addresses his defense of the Christians to the emperor Antoninus Pius, his sons, the Senate and the Roman people.

At Rome, Justin writes, those who come to believe pray and fast, and the community fasts with them. Then they are washed with water in the name of the Father, of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit. The washing is called illumination.

After baptism, Justin writes, the newly washed are brought to the gathering for prayer, and the believers greet one another with a kiss. Bread and a cup of wine mixed with water are brought to the one who presides. He gives thanks at length, the people say Amen, and deacons give to each and carry a share to those absent.
lines.reference: Justin, First Apology 65, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 16406-16436; Greek, cic/texts/justin-martyr_first-apology-grc_rauschen1911.txt lines 1707-1727

lines.text: Justin writes that this food is called eucharist, thanksgiving, and that only the baptized who live as Christ taught may share it. They receive it, he says, not as common bread and common drink.

On Sunday, Justin writes, all who live in town or country gather in one place. The memoirs of the apostles, which are called Gospels, or the writings of the prophets are read, the one who presides teaches, and all stand to pray.
lines.reference: Justin, First Apology 66-67, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 16477-16478, 16502-16509; Greek, cic/texts/justin-martyr_first-apology-grc_rauschen1911.txt lines 1759-1767

lines.text: At the Sunday gathering, those who are well off give what each chooses, and the one who presides uses it for orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers.
Justin says Christians meet on Sunday because on that first day God began his work of creation, and on the same day Jesus Christ rose from the dead.

At Justin's trial, the prefect Rusticus asks where the Christians gather. Justin answers that each meets where he chooses and can, and that he himself lives above one Martinus, at the Timiotinian Bath, and knows of no other meeting.
lines.note: From an anonymous account of the trial, of unknown date.

lines.text: Justin and his companions are scourged and beheaded.

timeline.when: When Soter was bishop of Rome
timeline.headline: Visitors and letters pass between Corinth and Rome

lines.when: before Anicetus was bishop of Rome
lines.text: Hegesippus, on his way to Rome, stays many days with the church of Corinth, then remains at Rome until Anicetus.
lines.note: Hegesippus's own words, as Eusebius keeps them.

lines.text: Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, praises Rome's custom from the beginning of sending gifts to churches in every city, and supplies to Christians in the mines, a custom Soter has kept and added to.
lines.note: Dionysius's own words, as Eusebius keeps them.

lines.text: Dionysius writes that Corinth read Rome's new letter on the Lord's holy day, and will always draw counsel from it, as from the earlier letter written through Clement.
lines.note: Dionysius's own words, as Eusebius keeps them.

timeline.when: Near the end of the 2nd century
timeline.headline: Rome's bishop tries to cut off the churches of Asia over the day of Easter
timeline.witness: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History, writing about a century later, with Irenaeus's own words

lines.when: while Eleutherius was bishop of Rome
lines.text: Irenaeus names Rome's bishops in order from the apostles to Eleutherius, a line by which, he writes, the apostles' tradition and the preaching of the truth have come down to his day.

lines.when: "the tenth year of the reign of Commodus"
lines.text: Victor becomes bishop of Rome.

The churches of all Asia, from an older tradition, end the fast before Easter on the moon's fourteenth day, the day of the Passover lamb. The other churches end it only on the day of the resurrection, the Lord's day.
Victor tries to cut off the churches of all Asia from the common unity, and writes letters declaring them all excommunicate.
Not all the bishops are pleased with Victor. They urge him to consider the things of peace, and some rebuke him sharply.
Irenaeus writes to Victor that the elders who led Rome before Soter did not keep the fourteenth day, yet lived at peace with visitors who did, and sent them the eucharist.
lines.note: Irenaeus's own words, as Eusebius keeps them.

lines.text: Irenaeus writes about the question to Victor and to most of the other leaders of the churches, a peacemaker, Eusebius says, true to his name.

timeline.headline: Their letters and their manual are still read

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Rome's letter to Corinth has been read publicly in a great many churches, both earlier and in his own day.
Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, sets "that which is called the Teaching of the Apostles, and the Shepherd" among the books the Fathers appointed to be read by newcomers to the faith.
Philotheos Bryennios finds, in a monastery library at Constantinople, a volume of manuscripts dated 1056. Among them is the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles.
lines.reference: Introductory notice to the Teaching, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 12522-12527, 12584-12586

lines.text: Bryennios publishes its text at Constantinople.
lines.reference: Introductory notice to the Teaching, cic/texts/anf07_lactantius-apostolic-constitutions-didache-liturgies.xml lines 12584-12586

briefSources.title: The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles (the Didache), in English
Rome's letter to Corinth, Ignatius's letters, Polycarp's letter, Justin's First Apology and Irenaeus's Against Heresies, in English

uncertain: Who led them. The old witnesses name their leaders differently. Ignatius urges a bishop presiding in the place of God, with the elders and the deacons. Rome's letter speaks of the same men as holding the bishop's office and as elders. Polycarp writes with "the presbyters with him" and does not call himself bishop, though Ignatius does. Hermas writes of the elders who preside and also of bishops. Irenaeus counts Rome's earlier leaders in the bishop's office from the apostles, and in his letter to Victor calls them elders who presided.

The thanksgiving. The witnesses describe it differently. The short manual gives thanks first over the cup, then over the bread. Justin tells of bread and a cup of wine mixed with water, with Jesus's words from the apostles' memoirs. Ignatius counts as proper only a thanksgiving the bishop leads, or one he entrusts.

Who wrote Rome's letter to Corinth. The letter is written in the name of the church of Rome. Dionysius of Corinth is the first held witness to say it was written through Clement, Irenaeus places the letter in Clement's time, and Eusebius says Clement wrote it in the church's name.
Pliny's account is a hostile outsider's. What he learned of their meetings came from people who had left them, and from two women under torture.
How the Easter quarrel ended. Eusebius records only that other bishops urged Victor to consider "the things of peace," and that Irenaeus wrote to make peace.

quotationOriginals.modern: On a fixed day they used to meet before dawn. They sang a hymn to Christ as to a god, taking turns among themselves.
quotationOriginals.printed: quod essent sohti stato die ante lucem convenire carmenque Christo quasi deo dicere secum invicem
quotationOriginals.work: Pliny, Letters 10.96.7 (Latin, in Carl Mirbt, Quellen zur Geschichte des Papsttums, 1911)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The scan reads sohti for soliti. A second held print of the same clause, in an editor's note in Ante-Nicene Fathers 5, reads soliti. Quasi deo is a pagan's phrase, as to a god; the 1890 English gives "as God".
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: they had been accustomed to come together on a fixed day before daylight and to sing responsively a song unto Christ as God

quotationOriginals.modern: On the day named after the Sun, all who live in the towns or in the country gather in one place. The memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, for as long as time allows.
quotationOriginals.printed: Καὶ τῇ τοῦ ἡλίου λεγομένῃ ἡμέρᾳ πάντων κατὰ πόλεις ἢ ἀγροὺς μενόντων ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ συνέλευσις γίνεται, καὶ τὰ ἀπομνημονεύματα τῶν ἀποστόλων ἢ τὰ συγγράμματα τῶν προφητῶν ἀναγινώσκεται, μέχρις ἐγχωρεῖ.
quotationOriginals.work: Justin Martyr, First Apology 67.3 (Greek, ed. Gerhard Rauschen, 1911; digital edition by the Perseus Project, Trustees of Tufts University, CC BY-SA 4.0)
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: And on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits;

quotationOriginals.modern: There are two ways, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life is this. First, you shall love God, who made you. Second, your neighbor as yourself.
quotationOriginals.printed: There are two ways, one of life and one of death; but a great difference between the two ways. 2. The way of life, then, is this: First, thou shalt love God who made thee; second, thy neighbour as thyself;
quotationOriginals.work: The Didache 1.1–2 (tr. Hall and Napier, Ante-Nicene Fathers 7, 1886)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek of the Didache is not held, so the English stands alone.
